notes.meaning: God speaks directly to Joshua after the death of Moses to confirm him as Israel's new leader. Joshua had served faithfully as Moses' assistant for decades, learning to lead by first learning how to obey. Even though a great human leader had died, God's work for His people went on without stopping.

The Lord tells Joshua that Moses is dead, so it is now time for him and all the people to cross the Jordan River. God was about to fulfill His promise and give Israel the land of Canaan. The death of a godly leader was not an excuse to give up, but a call to rise up and move forward.

God assures Joshua that He has already given Israel every piece of land where they set foot, just as He promised Moses long before. In God's eternal plan the land belonged to them, but they still had to step out and claim it. God's promises give us confidence to step forward and do what He commands.

The Lord outlines the full borders of the territory, reaching from the southern wilderness to Lebanon in the north, and from the Euphrates River in the east to the Mediterranean Sea in the west. This vast region included all the lands ruled by the Canaanite nations, here represented by the Hittites. God gave them a real, physical homeland, though Israel would not occupy all of it until the reigns of King David and King Solomon.

God promises Joshua that no enemy will be able to stand against him throughout his entire life. The Lord pledges to be with Joshua just as He was with Moses, never abandoning him or leaving him without help. Israel's upcoming victories would not come from military might, but from God's faithful presence.

The Lord commands Joshua to be strong and courageous because he will lead the nation to possess the land promised to their ancestors. Leading such a large and often stubborn people was a heavy burden, and Joshua may have felt inadequate compared to Moses. God called him to be brave, resting on the sure promise of God rather than his own abilities.

Joshua is told again to be very courageous, with a focus on obeying all the laws God gave through Moses. He must not stray from God's commands to the right or to the left, but follow them faithfully in every decision. True success in God's work comes only through careful and total obedience to His revealed word.

God commands Joshua to keep the Book of the Law constantly on his lips and to think about it day and night. A leader cannot govern God's people well without continually studying and practicing God's word. Obeying the Scriptures would make his path prosperous and give him wise success in all his duties.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teachers treat this verse as a general formula for personal financial wealth and worldly success.

notes.meaning: God reminds Joshua with a powerful question that this mission comes directly from His own divine command. Joshua has no reason to be terrified or discouraged, because the Lord his God will go with him everywhere. The constant presence of the almighty God is greater than any danger or enemy we might face.

Having received God's instructions, Joshua steps forward immediately to lead the nation. He gives orders to the officers who assisted the tribes and managed official announcements. Joshua's prompt action showed his faith in the promises God had just spoken to him.

Joshua instructs the officers to tell the people to prepare their travel food because they will cross the Jordan River in three days. Even though God was still feeding them with manna, they needed to gather meat and grain from the conquered territory for their march. Trusting God's promises goes hand in hand with making practical, orderly preparations.

Joshua turns specifically to address the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. These groups had asked for and received pasture land on the east side of the Jordan River before Moses died. Before the army moved out, Joshua called on them to honor their unique commitment.

Joshua reminds these eastern tribes of the command Moses gave them when they received their land. God had granted them rest from their wilderness travels and given them good cities to live in. Yet their settlement came with a duty to assist the rest of Israel before settling down in comfort.

Their wives, children, and livestock were permitted to stay safe in the homes Moses had given them east of the river. However, their armed warriors were required to march across the Jordan ahead of the other tribes to help them fight. Because their own homes were already secure, it was only fair that they should take the lead in helping their brothers.

These soldiers were to remain in the war until the Lord gave the other tribes rest and full possession of their land. Only when the whole nation had secured its inheritance could the eastern fighters return home to enjoy their own territory. God's people must never turn away from helping others just because their own needs have already been met.

The leaders of the eastern tribes answer Joshua with complete willingness, promising to do everything he commands. They gladly agree to go wherever he sends them in battle and to support the entire nation. Their eager reply showed their recognition of Joshua as God's chosen leader.

The eastern tribes promise to obey Joshua just as they had listened to Moses during the wilderness journey. They also offer a heartfelt prayer asking the Lord to be with Joshua and prosper him as He had with Moses. Their obedience was offered in the confident hope that God would guide their new leader in all things.

The tribes agree that anyone who rebels against Joshua's authority or refuses to obey his battle orders will be put to death. Strict military order was essential to preserve unity and prevent dangerous mutiny as they entered hostile enemy lands. They finish by echoing God's own words back to Joshua, urging their commander to be strong and courageous.
